NFS2ROOT (CVE-2026-99362): pre-auth remote root in the Linux NFS server. Fixed in Debian trixie, Ubuntu still vulnerable. How to check your boxes  If any of your servers or your NAS share folders over NFS, this one is worth five minutes today.  CVE-2026-99362, named NFS2ROOT by the researchers at OpenSec, is a flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server (nfsd). Per their write-up it goes back to Linux 3.16 and affects hosts that export NFSv4.1 or 4.2 with tcp/2049 reachable. Red Hat rates it Critical: an unauthenticated remote attacker can corrupt kernel memory, which means root with no login. OpenSec says it is keeping its exploit private, and nobody reports it being exploited yet.  Where the fixes are, as of today:  - Upstream: 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (per OpenSec) - Debian trixie: fixed from 6.12.117. Bookworm's default 6.1 kernel is still vulnerable, but bookworm's 6.12 kernel is fixed. - Ubuntu: rated Critical (CVSS 9.8), and every supported release still shows "Vulnerable". No USN yet. - Red Hat: Critical, no fix listed yet. Default RHEL doesn't run nfsd at all.  So on Ubuntu, apt upgrade won't help yet. First check whether you're exposed at all:      systemctl is-active nfs-server     sudo exportfs -v     cat /proc/fs/nfsd/versions  If nfs-server isn't active and nothing is exported, this one doesn't affect that box. If the versions file shows +4.1 or +4.2, read on.  If you don't need NFS on that machine, turn it off:      sudo systemctl disable --now nfs-server  If you do need it, make sure 2049 only answers your own clients. With ufw, for example:      sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 2049 proto tcp     sudo ufw deny 2049/tcp  (Change the subnet to your LAN, and check the rule order with sudo ufw status numbered.) This is also Red Hat's mitigation: disable the NFS server if you don't need it, or restrict port 2049 to trusted networks.  Question for the NAS crowd: has anyone seen a statement from TrueNAS SCALE, OpenMediaVault, Unraid or Synology about this? They all run Linux-based NFS servers, and I haven't found anything from them yet. Your magic link gets clicked before your user ever sees it.  Corporate mail gateways open every link in an incoming email to check it for malware. If your link spends its token on a GET, the scanner signs in and the real person gets "Link expired". They ask for a new one, the scanner eats that one too, and they give up.  The tell is in your logs: Gmail users are fine, and everyone on a company or school domain fails.  Let the link open a page and let a button do the signing in:  GET  /auth/confirm?token=...  renders a Sign in button, changes nothing POST /auth/confirm            spends the token  A scanner reads pages, but it doesn't press buttons.  How to steal it: 1. Make every GET and HEAD on auth and confirm links side-effect free. 2. Put a 6-digit code in the same email as the fallback, since scanners can't type. 3. Don't raise the expiry, the scanner gets there seconds after delivery anyway.  Which of your emails has a link that spends a token on GET?

The agent probed the infrastructure, went away for 11 hours, then came back with an exploit.  Timing how long the exploit code took to run is absolutely ridiculous.  To make an analogy: it's like someone writing an essay, timing how long it took them to physically hand it in to the professor, then saying "completing the essay took 1.3 seconds".  While technically correct (the essay was not completed until it was handed in). Any reasonable person is going to thinking "completing an essay" means from start to finish.  AI can do some tasks very fast. But these types of metrics are intentionally misleading. They're designed to spread FUD and delude people about how fast AI attacks actually are.  ARTEX did not hack the admin account in 1.3 seconds. ARTEX spend 11 hours developing attack tools and one of the tools took 1.3 seconds to run (that's actually fairly slow for code, but not unreasonable).  The point of focus should be that the AI was able to weaponize a vulnerability in 11 hours (it would likely take a human much longer), not that the exploit took 1.3 second to run (it would take a human the exact same amount of time).

I have this investigation where an employee downloaded malware, then the website was deleted from their browsing history.  The way browsing history works is similar to hard drives. When you delete something, it doesn't get erased, the space is just marked as unused. The actual data stay put until the space is needed for something else, at which point it gets overwritten.  It's very annoying because I can still see exactly which website was responsible for the malware infection, because that data is still there, but because the database record was unlinked, all the metadata is gone.  So I can't offer a  nice neat "X led to Y which led to Z" type explanation. I just have to be like "well these two things happened, and that implies that maybe this other thing happened, but correlation does not equal causation"😭

You can tell who doesn't work in cybersecurity, because they're convinced it's a great time to be in the industry because "more cyberattacks means more cybersecurity spending".  It's a great time to be a shareholder, and that's about it.   I am not aware of a single company that operates on the basis of "cyberattacks are up 10%, we need to hire 10% more defenders".  What actually happens, is 10% more cyberattacks means 10% more work for the same pay. And the workload just keeps increasing until people end up burning out and quitting, or worse.  At some point if things get bad enough, a company may, and that is a very heavy lifting "may", find budget for additional headcount.  But, like, go find me someone who works in cyber defense and isn't burnt out, and I'll find you someone who doesn't do any work.  Cybersecurity is one of those industries where IMO the salaries only look good on paper.   If you're coming from a minimum wage customer service job, it's definitely a huge improvement. But if you're going into white collar work anyway, there's so many jobs that pay well and won't burn you out.

Coding makes companies money, cybersecurity loses companies money. By what metric will cybersecurity ever be a bigger industry that coding?  Greg should attend a board meeting at basically any company, probably even his own, and try asking them for $100 to buy Yubikeys.
